title: Reading assembly notation
intro: The assembler turns assembly text into machine instructions. Directives give the assembler directions; labels name positions in the program. Neither runs as an instruction.

lines.explanation: Selects the code section, where the assembler places the instructions that follow.
Makes the name reference_example available to other assembled files when the linker joins them. .globl is another spelling of .global.
Defines a label at this position. Here it names the first instruction's address. reference_example is a name chosen for this example, not a reserved command.

note: .global alone does not choose where execution starts or call the code. This course's supplied linker script selects _start as the program's entry point, the address where xv6 starts your program.
preparedNote: In lesson fragments, the lab supplies entry, capture and exit code. Edit the lesson's instructions; you do not need to add this header. Complete-program projects include their own entry code.
pseudoNote: A pseudo-instruction is assembler shorthand for one or more machine instructions. The recorded examples show before and after the whole source line, including every instruction it expands into.

placeholders.explanation: A destination register: the register that receives the result.
Source registers: the registers whose values the instruction reads.
An immediate: a number written directly in the instruction. Each instruction's rules give the allowed range.
A memory address formed by adding the written byte offset to the address in the base register.
A name defined with a colon, such as retry:. Use the name without the colon in a branch or jump.
